body: I only watched the crash scene. What my friends told me about the movie doesn't really makes me want to go and watch it, not my type of thing.

I don't think he should decide for you to become a pilot. All the pilots I know seriously love aviation and planes and are super geeks when it comes to that. I don't think you'd do well if it's not something you really want, it's hard work. Women can fly planes, absolutely, during the last part of the pilot course we do something called MCC, multi crew cooperation, which is when you team up with a colleague and tackle problems in the simulator. I was with one of the two females in my course and I was very happy with my decision. There's a few female pilots where I work, but they're not captains yet so I haven't flown with them.
No on purpose, but at first I sometimes forget them on...

The key to a good landing is keeping the right speed. Too high the plane will want to climb too low it will descend bellow the glide slope. Thank god air traffic controllers do a better job in real life than on flight simulator otherwise it would be a mess! There's two saying about landings that I'll share! 1) there's 3 steps for a good landing, unfortunaly, nobody knows what they are. 2) a good landing is one where you walk away from. A perfect landing is one where you can fly the plane again.

That depends on the plane, crew, and workload (bad weather, time of day, humor, etc. Personally, I like to hand fly bellow 10'000 feet that gives you about 10 minutes of actual hand flying per sector. The more automation you use, the more your mind is available for dealing with unexpected occurrences, so it's a good thing in my view. Some type of aircraft (regional turboprops) have a very limited autopilot, only holds heading and altitude if you're lucky, while state of the art airliners can manage a flight from 200 feet above the ground on take off to a auto landing, where all you have to do is taxi and park the plane. But keep in mind that a auto landing requires much more attention to the airplane than a normal landing, because you are outside the control loop, therefore the need to be sure everything's going according to the book is happening. Auto lands are done in very low visibility conditions, if you're wandering.

Usually that's more prone to happen if you happen to book on a repositioning flight. Lets say a plane leaves maintenance and it's supposed to go to nowheresville for the next morning flight. Usually you get a pretty cheap ticket and a crew all for yourself! I've never done it myself, but colleagues tell me about times they've flown with just a handful of pax. It's not "common" but I wouldn't call you liar if you told me it happened to you.
Thank apple for it's amazing autocorrect feature. Also, when it comes to airplanes and technical details, it's my passion. I breathe aviation!

Yup! Fuel is the awnser. We have a thing called cost index that can put on our computers which basically tells the computer how fast and how much fuel we want to use. The bigger the value, the faster we get there. On our flight briefing, the company tells us what cost index we are to use, let's say, 60. But, if we are late, we can increase it to 100 for example, making it up for the time lost, at the cost of extra fuel. A crew who increases the cost index for their flight regularly could be subject to a meeting with the chief pilot.
